original_item.title: Owner authorization on fee configuration (OUT OF SCOPE)

reviewed_items.reasoning: The counterexample attack (non-role-holder calling setFeeParams) is correctly prevented by the onlyRole(FEE_MANAGER_ROLE) modifier at LiquidityManager.sol:184. The OpenZeppelin AccessControl implementation reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount when a caller lacks the required role. Additionally, validateFeeParams() at IncentiveLib.sol:183-191 enforces parameter bounds: (1) targetLiquidity <= MAX_TARGET_LIQUIDITY (2^128-1), (2) k <= K_BPS_DENOM (10000 = 100%), and (3) arithmetic overflow prevention via maxK check. Even if an attacker somehow obtained FEE_MANAGER_ROLE, parameter validation prevents dangerous configurations. This item is also marked OUT OF SCOPE per the trust model, as FEE_MANAGER operations are trusted.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample scenario (non-admin calling setFeeParams) is NOT plausible because the onlyRole modifier is correctly implemented and enforced. OpenZeppelin's AccessControl is a battle-tested implementation. The attack would immediately revert.

guards_found.reason: OpenZeppelin AccessControl enforces role-based access control. Non-role-holders cannot bypass.
Validates targetLiquidity bounds, k bounds, and prevents arithmetic overflow in fee calculations.
FEE_MANAGER_ROLE is granted to initialOwner during initialize(), ensuring only trusted parties have access.

guard_analysis.bypass_method: None identified. OpenZeppelin AccessControl has no known bypass vulnerabilities.

original_item.title: Proof soundness guarantees validity at on-chain verification

counterexample.scenario: Malicious prover generates forged proof to mint tokens

guards_identified: require() wrapper on all verification calls

reviewed_items.reasoning: The counterexample (malicious prover generating forged proof) is NOT plausible due to the cryptographic soundness guarantees of the ZK proof system. At Verifier.sol:275, 326, and 348, all proof submissions are verified using on-chain verifier contracts via require() statements: (1) IRootDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof() for transfer root proofs, (2) IWithdrawDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof() for Nova teleport proofs, (3) IWithdrawVerifier.verifyProof() for Groth16 single teleport proofs. These verifier contracts implement cryptographic verification (Nova IVC folding or Groth16 pairing checks) that cannot be forged without breaking the discrete logarithm assumption on BN254 or the hash function collision resistance. The require() wrapper ensures any invalid proof causes immediate transaction revert with InvalidProof() error. The prover is UNTRUSTED by design - security is guaranteed by ZKP soundness, not prover trust.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: Generating a valid ZK proof for false statements requires breaking the cryptographic assumptions underlying Nova/Groth16. The ZK proof system guarantees computational soundness - a polynomial-time adversary cannot produce valid proofs for false statements except with negligible probability. The counterexample attack would fail at the verification step.

guards_found.reason: Nova IVC proof verification is cryptographically sound. Invalid proofs rejected.
Nova IVC proof verification for withdrawal proofs. Cryptographic soundness guaranteed.
Groth16 pairing-based proof verification. BN254 curve security guarantees soundness.

guard_analysis.bypass_method: None. Bypassing would require breaking the cryptographic assumptions (discrete log on BN254, hash collision resistance).

original_item.title: Groth16 proof structure matches on-chain verifier expectations

counterexample.scenario: Submit proof with wrong curve point encoding
preconditions: Have proof bytes with invalid G1/G2 point encoding
attack_steps: abi.decode succeeds but verifier rejects invalid curve points
counterexample.actual_behavior: Groth16 verifier validates curve points as part of verification

guards_identified: abi.decode with fixed types at Verifier.sol:313, 343-344

reviewed_items.reasoning: The counterexample (submitting malformed proof bytes) is correctly handled by multiple layers of validation. At Verifier.sol:344-345, abi.decode expects specific types: (uint256[2], uint256[2][2], uint256[2], uint256[3]). Malformed bytes with incorrect length cause abi.decode to revert. If the bytes decode successfully but contain invalid curve points (not on BN254 curve), the Groth16 verifier contract at line 348 will reject them during the ecMul/ecAdd/ecPairing operations. These EVM precompiles return 0 on invalid inputs, causing the verification to fail. Additionally, the Nova proof paths at lines 267 (uint256[32]) and 314 (uint256[34]) have fixed-size decoding that rejects malformed inputs. The proof structure enforcement is complete and no malformed proof can pass verification.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: Malformed proof bytes are rejected at multiple levels: (1) abi.decode reverts on length mismatch, (2) EVM precompiles reject invalid curve points, (3) verifier contracts reject proofs that don't satisfy the verification equation. No path allows malformed proofs to succeed.

guards_found.reason: Fixed-size type decoding ensures exact byte length. Shorter calldata causes revert.
Nova proof must decode to exactly 32 uint256 values. Structure enforced.
Withdrawal Nova proof must decode to exactly 34 uint256 values. Structure enforced.
ecAdd, ecMul, ecPairing precompiles validate curve points. Invalid points fail silently (return 0), causing verification failure.

guard_analysis.bypass_method: None. abi.decode and EVM precompiles enforce correct structure and curve point validity.

original_item.title: Merkle proof validity guaranteed by ZK circuit verification

counterexample.scenario: Malicious indexer provides false Merkle path to user
attack_steps: User generates ZK proof with wrong Merkle path
counterexample.expected_result: Cannot generate valid proof with invalid Merkle path
counterexample.actual_behavior: ZK circuit enforces Merkle path validity

guards_identified: Transfer root public input binding at Verifier.sol:366-368

reviewed_items.reasoning: The counterexample (malicious indexer providing false Merkle path) cannot lead to a security breach. The Merkle path is verified inside the ZK circuit during proof generation, not on-chain. If the indexer provides incorrect Merkle siblings, the circuit constraints become unsatisfiable - the computed root won't match the expected root embedded in the circuit. The prover cannot generate a valid proof for an invalid Merkle path. Even if somehow a proof was generated, the transfer root is a public input that is verified on-chain at Verifier.sol:367-369: `require(expectedRoot == transferRoot, TransferRootMismatch(...))`. The root must match either provedTransferRoots[rootHint] or globalTransferRoots[rootHint], which are set only by verified proofs or Hub relay. An indexer providing bad data causes proof generation failure (denial of service to the user), not a security vulnerability. The indexer is SEMI_TRUSTED - they can deny service but cannot cause incorrect minting.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The attack sequence cannot succeed. Wrong Merkle siblings cause proof generation to fail at the client side. The ZK circuit enforces that the Merkle path hashes to the claimed root. No valid proof can be generated for an incorrect path.

guards_found.reason: Circuit enforces that hashing siblings along the path produces the claimed root. Invalid path = unsatisfiable constraints.
expectedRoot must match transferRoot from proof public inputs. Root checked against provedTransferRoots or globalTransferRoots.
Prevents claiming tokens against non-existent roots.

guard_analysis.bypass_method: None. Merkle path validity is cryptographically enforced by ZK circuit. On-chain root verification provides defense in depth.

ZK circuit - Computes hash chain from leaf to root using provided siblings
ZK circuit - If computed root != expected root, constraints unsatisfied, proof generation fails
Verifier.sol:367 - On-chain: expectedRoot = isGlobal ? globalTransferRoots[rootHint] : provedTransferRoots[rootHint]
Verifier.sol:369 - require(expectedRoot == transferRoot, TransferRootMismatch(...))
reviewed_items.notes: Indexer is SEMI_TRUSTED. Invalid Merkle data causes proof generation failure (liveness issue), not security breach. ZK soundness prevents invalid paths from producing valid proofs.

original_item.title: Merkle structure matches on-chain hash chain computation

counterexample.scenario: Indexer uses keccak256 instead of SHA-256
preconditions: Indexer misconfigured to use wrong hash
attack_steps: User requests Merkle proof from indexer
ZK proof generated with wrong leaf values
counterexample.actual_behavior: Hash mismatch causes proof failure, not incorrect minting

guards_identified: ZK circuit must use matching hash function

reviewed_items.reasoning: The counterexample (indexer using wrong hash function) cannot lead to a security breach - it only causes proof failure. The on-chain hash chain computation uses ShaHashChainLib.sol:7-9 which implements SHA-256 with 248-bit truncation: `sha256(abi.encodePacked(prev, from, to, value)) & 0x00FF...`. This hash is used to compute the on-chain hash chain state stored in zERC20. The ZK circuit must use the identical hash function (SHA-256 with 248-bit truncation) to produce valid proofs. If the indexer uses a different hash function, the leaf values computed by the indexer won't match what's recorded on-chain. When the user generates a ZK proof, the circuit will fail because the Merkle path won't hash to the expected root. This is a configuration/integration concern, not a security vulnerability - mismatched hashes result in proof failure, not incorrect minting. The defense is that any mismatch causes the proof to be invalid.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: Hash function mismatch causes proof failure, not security breach. The attack sequence ends with 'proof verification fails on-chain' - this is the correct and safe behavior. No tokens can be incorrectly minted.

guards_found.reason: On-chain uses sha256 with 248-bit truncation. This is the canonical definition that indexer and ZK circuit must match.
All on-chain hash chain updates use the same library, ensuring consistency.
ZK circuit must implement identical hash. Mismatch causes proof generation failure, not security breach.

guard_analysis.bypass_method: None. Hash mismatch causes proof failure. Security is preserved even with misconfigured indexer.
